en: The definition of compounds—Śrī Ratnamaṇḍanasūri:
A *dvandva* compound is that which begins with the sound of the nominative case; it is either *itaretara* (copulative) or *samāhāra* (collective).
The former retains its own gender and number, while the latter is neuter and ends in the singular. (1)

*Prathamā* and *ca*, and *prathamā* and *ca*: these two pairs form *prathamācau*. Those sounds or words (*dhvani*) which have *prathamācau* at their beginning are called *prathamācāgra*. That [text] in which such sounds exist is *pra* (i.e., *prathamācāgradhvani*).

That *dvandva* (copulative compound) is of two kinds. Which? The *itaretara* (mutual) and again, which? The *samāhāra* (collective). By this much, the two-fold nature of the *dvandva* has been stated. "Having its own gender and number" means that the gender is determined with respect to the final word, and the number is determined with respect to the number of the things expressed. For example: *netre ca nāsikā ca* (the eyes and the nose) becomes *netranāsikāḥ*; *dhavaśca khadiraśca palāśaśca* (the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees) becomes *dhavakhadirapalāśāḥ*;
*uttamaśca madhyamaśca adhamaśca* (the highest, middle, and lowest) becomes *uttamamadhyamādhamāḥ*. This [last] is a masculine (*puruṣa*) term consisting solely of qualifiers.
Now, the collective compound (*samāhāra*): *aśvaśca vaḍavā ca* (a horse and a mare) becomes *aśvavaḍavam*; *gāvaśca mahiṣāśca* (cows and buffaloes) becomes *gaumahiṣam*, and so forth. [Commentary 1]

O wise one, first identify the two—the quality and the possessor of the quality—along with their respective gender and number; then, having combined them using the middle-case forms of the pronouns *tad* and *adaḥ*, compose your *karmadhāraya* compound.

Pratha0: O Budha, you [should understand] that "guṇaguṇinau" (quality and the possessor of quality) and "viśeṣaṇaviśeṣye" (qualifier and the qualified) are to be compounded in a *karmadhāraya* compound. (With apprehension: Of what kind? "Prathamācāgrau"—that is, those two before whom there is both the nominative case (*prathamā*) and the word "ca" (*caśca*). The meaning is: the two *ca*s that connect words ending in the nominative case. By means of which two? Madhya0: "Tadadasau"—that is, by those two which are situated in the middle and are "tad" and "adas. This inclusion of "tad" is for the purpose of including the word "adas" as well, when it ends in the masculine singular nominative.

By what two [words]? By those two whose gender and number are identical to that of the *viśeṣya* (the qualificand), which is the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*). For example: he is both a hero and a man, thus "hero-man" (*vīrapuruṣaḥ*); she is both sweet and speech, thus "sweet-speech" (*madhuravāṇī*); that is both clear and a face, thus "clear-face" (*prasannavadanam*). The same applies to the remaining cases of number. Furthermore, by intention (*vivakṣayā*), even the qualificand may become the qualifier; therefore, he is both the navel and the king, thus "navel-king" (*nābhinṛpaḥ*). Such is the *karmadhāraya* compound. Commentary 2.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, words beginning with numerals and "near" (*āsanna*), as well as others together with words for directions (*dig*) and sub-directions (*diśā*), and all those beginning with "equal to the qualities" (*guṇisama-sāman*), when joined with other numerals, become compounds. Commentary: The connection is that words beginning with numerals and "near," when joined with numeral words (*saṃkhyā-śabda*), become complete compounds. "Numerals" refers to words denoting numbers, and these, together with those beginning with "near," form a *dvandva* compound. Here, by the word "beginning" (*pramukha*), words meaning "near," such as "not far" (*adūra*) and "exceeding" (*adhika*), are included. For example: *dvirdaśa* (twice ten) = *dvidaśāḥ* (twenty). Similarly, *tridaśāḥ* and so forth. Also, *dvau vā trayo vā* (two or three) = *dvitrāḥ*.

In this manner, for "three," "four," and so on, the suffix *ḍa* is applied everywhere according to the rule *pramāṇī-saṃkhyā-ḍaḥ*. Those of whom there are nine or eleven are called *āsannadaśāḥ* (those near ten). Likewise, there are terms such as *nikaṭanavāḥ* (near nine) and *adūradaśāḥ* (not far from ten). A word denoting a cardinal direction, when joined with another word denoting a cardinal direction, forms a compound; for example, that which is the intermediate space between the northern and eastern directions is *uttarapūrvā*, i.e., the northeast (*aiśānī*). In this way, the specific intermediate directions (*vidiś*) are also to be expressed. The word *saha* ("with") is joined with all words, as follows:

It exists together with a son, thus it is *saputraḥ* (with a son). In the same way, [words] such as *savidya* (with knowledge) and so forth are also formed. Other words that exclude *saha* (together with) are joined with all [other] words. By what means? Having brought them into agreement (*sāma*) regarding their qualities (*guṇa*), the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is the qualificand; by this, it means that [the word] has the same gender and number. It exists only when accompanied by the six case-endings beginning with the accusative (*amādi*), starting from the second case. This is the rule for *sāmādi*. Furthermore, there is a *dvandva* compound of the two qualifiers: "that which is equal to the possessor of the quality" (*guṇisama*) and "that which begins with *sāmādi*" (*sāmādi*). Then, by the phrase "where that *guṇisamasāmādi* [occurs]," [the rule applies].

The meaning is that everything [as the first member] is compounded with all [words as the second member] by means of a word ending in the accusative case or others, provided the gender and number are identical. For example: *uccairmukhaḥ* (one whose face is high), *udyauvanaḥ kumāraḥ* (a youth whose youth has emerged). Similarly, *udraśmi* and others have indeclinables (*avyaya*) as their prior members. *Natendraḥ pārśvaḥ* (Pārśva, by whom Indra was bowed); *jitamoho jinaḥ* (the Jina, by whom delusion was conquered); *dattadakṣiṇo dvijaḥ* (the twice-born to whom a sacrificial fee was given).

3. One from whom passion has departed is a "passionless one" (*vītarāga*), [as in] the Victor (*jina*). 4. That which has cool rays is the "cool-rayed one" (*śītaraśmi*), [as in] the moon (*indu*). 5. That in which sprouts have appeared is the "earth with appeared sprouts" (*prādurbhūtāṅkurā bhūḥ*). 6. These variations in the *bahuvrīhi* compound arise through the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*). One whose mind is on the Dharma is "Dharma-minded" (*dharmamati*). That from which the destruction of suffering arises is "the destruction of suffering" (*duḥkhakṣaya*). These and others are variations that occur even without the relationship of qualifier and qualified. Commentary 3.

When words ending in the seven case-terminations are compounded with a word ending in the nominative case, that compound is called *tatpuruṣa*. It takes the gender of the subsequent member (*paraliṅga*), like the *anaṃtara* (the *bahuvrīhi*) which follows;

thus, the *tatpuruṣa* consists of two principal words. *Sapta0*: "That compound" means that in which the gender of the subsequent member prevails. Like the *anaṃtara*, namely the *bahuvrīhi*, it takes the gender of the subsequent member. The meaning is that both the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa* take the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣya*). *Mukhya*: "Two principal words. For example: * **Nominative:** *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* → *rājapuruṣaḥ* (King's man) * **Accusative:** *rājñaḥ puruṣam* → *rājapuruṣam* (King's man) * **Instrumental:** *rājñā puruṣeṇa* → *rājapuruṣeṇa* (By the king's man) * **Dative:** *rājñe puruṣāya* → *rājapuruṣāya* (To the king's man) * **Ablative:** *rājñaḥ puruṣāt* → *rājapuruṣāt* (From the king's man) * **Genitive:** *rājñaḥ puruṣasya* → *rājapuruṣasya* (Of the king's man) * **Locative:** *rājñi puruṣe* → *rājapuruṣe* (In the king's man)

"Bhavasāgara" means the ocean that is existence itself. "Susādhu" means one who is excellent or virtuous. "Candravatsaumya" means gentle like the moon. "Ajita" means not conquered. In such cases as these, there is a first-case (nominative) tatpuruṣa compound. (1) "Vṛkṣārūḍha" means one who has climbed a tree. "Atikhaṭva" means one who has passed beyond a bedstead. This is a second-case (accusative) tatpuruṣa compound. (2) "Guṇayukta" means endowed with qualities. "Parivīrut" means surrounded by creepers. This is a third-case (instrumental) tatpuruṣa compound. (3)

Beneficial for living beings is *jīvahita* (a genitive tatpuruṣa). One who is exhausted with regard to study is *paryadhyayana* (a fourth-case [dative] tatpuruṣa). 4. Fearing evil is *pāpabhīta* (a fifth-case [ablative] tatpuruṣa). Departed from Kauśāmbī is *niṣkauśāṃbi* (a fifth-case [ablative] tatpuruṣa). 5. The king’s man is *rājapuruṣa* (a sixth-case [genitive] tatpuruṣa). Half of a pepper is *ardhapippalī* (a sixth-case [genitive] tatpuruṣa). 6. Steadfast in dharma is *dharmadhīra* (a seventh-case [locative] tatpuruṣa). 7. || Commentary 4 ||

An *avyayībhāva* compound, whose prior member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and which primarily denotes that [indeclinable's] meaning, is neuter. After a neuter ending in a vowel other than *a*, there is elision (*lup*) of the case-ending; furthermore, in this [compound], the augment *āt* is added after [the final vowel] except for the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

Avyayībhāva compound: [The suffix *am* is applied] after a word ending in *a*, excluding those ending in *a* [when it follows a word] other than one ending in *a*. [This applies] to the beginning [of the compound], excluding the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: "near a jar" (*upakumbham*) and "near a garland" (*upamālam*) exist; [one] sees (1), shines (2), becomes angry (3); "near a jar" (*upakumbhāt*), O sinless one, there is beauty (5), [and one] lies down. Likewise, "near a virtuous person" (*upasādhu*); "near a wife" (*upavadhu*), "near a river" (*upanadi*). Examples include "in front of the face" (*yathāmukham*), "daily" (*pratyaham*), "offering of strength" (*balisuram*), and so forth. Commentary 5.
In a *dvigu* compound, a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expressing a number is the qualifier for the collective whole;
it takes the singular number and, depending on whether it ends in a short vowel or a long vowel, it takes either the neuter gender or the feminine gender.

When it is stated that the specific [word] following a numeral-denoting term ends in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it follows that the qualifier also takes the sixth case ending. The intention is that in a *dvigu* compound, after a word ending in the sixth case, one should employ the word "collection" (*samāhāra*) which refers solely to the object qualified by the preceding numeral. For example, the collection of the three worlds is *trilokī*. Compounds such as *pañcarājī* (five kings) are formed in the same way. After a word ending in *ā*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is optionally applied; for instance, the collection of three garlands is *trimālā* or *trimālam*.
Thus, there is a neuter gender for these words ending in *i* and so forth, as in examples such as *dvimuni*, *dvinadi*, and *trijagat*. (Commentary 6)

Thus ends the sixfold definition of compounds composed by Śrī Ratnamaṇḍana. Written by Līlā in the city of Ṣayarana on the first day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna in the year 16 [of the Śaka era], beginning from Āṣāḍha 17, for the purpose of recitation by Muni Ṛddhivijaya.
Thus ends the section on the formation of the six types of compounds.
Thus has been written the *Samāsalakṣaṇa* composed by the venerable master Ratnamaṇḍana Sūri. May there be prosperity!

Whatever herein I have written that is incorrect or contrary to the scriptures, all of that should be corrected by the illustrious and eminent masters, having bestowed their grace upon me. May there be prosperity!
